titel: Credit reports, credit scores and keeping your finances in order
kurz: How accounts and payment behaviour turn into a credit score in the US, what a weak score costs in interest, and which precautions keep your finances working even in an emergency.

bloecke.md: Every contract in which one side performs first is a form of credit. Examples are the apartment before the first rent payment, the phone plan with a financed handset, buy now, pay later, the car loan and the credit card. The side that performs first wants to know how likely it is to get its money back. To find out, it asks a credit bureau, not the person concerned. [[Creditworthiness]] is therefore not a judgement of character. It determines the terms you are offered, and in the US it is also checked by landlords, by insurers in most states and, with your written permission, by some employers.

## What a credit report contains

The three nationwide credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, collect data on credit accounts and payment behaviour. A credit report lists credit cards, loans, mortgages and other credit accounts with their limits, balances and age, whether payments were made on time, accounts in collection, bankruptcies and the inquiries made by lenders. Income, savings, checking account balances, race, religion and nationality do not appear in it.

A poor score is therefore almost always the result of late payments, high balances or a short history, not of a low income. A high salary does not improve it either, because salary does not appear in this data. Salary only plays a role when the lender asks for it in its own application to check your ability to repay.

Besides the three bureaus, there are specialty consumer reporting agencies. ChexSystems and Early Warning Services hold data on closed and overdrawn bank accounts, tenant screening companies compile reports for landlords, and other databases record insurance claims. An incorrect entry may therefore be sitting in a database you have never checked.

The first misconception is: "I earn well, so my credit is good." But income is not part of the credit report and can never make up for a weak score.

The second misconception is: "I'll tidy up and close old cards." Closing a card removes its credit limit, so the share of available credit you use (utilization) rises. Later, when the closed account drops off the report, your credit history also becomes shorter. An old card without an annual fee is often best kept open and used occasionally.

The third misconception is: "You have to carry a balance to build credit." Paying the full statement balance every month builds the same payment history and costs no interest.

## How the score is calculated

A [[Credit score|credit score]] describes a comparison group, not an individual person. It estimates how likely people with a similar credit report are to fall seriously behind on payments. The most widely used scores are FICO and VantageScore, both mostly on a scale from 300 to 850. According to FICO, payment history accounts for about 35% of the score, amounts owed for 30%, length of credit history for 15%, new credit for 10% and the mix of credit types for 10%. There are many versions, including industry-specific scores for auto loans and credit cards, so the same person has a different score with a car dealer than with a card issuer.

If a lender denies your application or offers worse terms because of your credit report, it must send you an adverse action notice. It names the credit bureau, entitles you to a free copy of the report within 60 days, and under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act you can request the specific reasons for a denial. Lenders may not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status or age, or because your income comes from public assistance.

bloecke.unter: The credit bureaus sit between the creditors that report data and the parties that query it; you deal with each side separately, and your direct access to the stored data is the free credit report.

## Interest costs with weak credit

A weak score rarely leads only to a rejection; usually it leads to a higher interest rate. Personal loans are offered at very different [[Annual percentage rate (APR)|APRs]] depending on the score, and credit card rates commonly exceed 20%. bloecke.titel: Soft inquiry instead of hard inquiry
bloecke.md: Checking your own credit and prequalification offers create a **soft inquiry**, which has no effect on your score. A loan or card application creates a **hard inquiry**. It can lower a FICO score by a few points, stays on the report for two years and is counted for one year. For mortgages, auto loans and student loans, several inquiries within a short shopping window (14 to 45 days, depending on the score version) count as one, so comparing offers is not punished. This does not apply to credit card applications. Before applying, ask whether a lender's quote uses a soft or a hard pull. This check costs nothing.

## How long negative items stay

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, most negative information may be reported for seven years and a bankruptcy for up to ten years. For late payments, charge-offs and collections, the seven years run from the date of the original delinquency, not from the date you pay. Paying an old collection therefore does not restart the clock, but it does not remove the entry early either; newer score versions, however, ignore paid collections. The credit bureaus also no longer report paid medical collections or medical collections under $500.

The credit reporting period is separate from the statute of limitations, the state-law deadline after which a creditor can no longer win a lawsuit over a debt. In some states, a partial payment on an old debt can restart that deadline.

bloecke.titel: How long entries stay on a credit report
bloecke.unter: Figures in months. Seven and ten years are maximum periods under the Fair Credit Reporting Act; the periods for Chapter 13 bankruptcy and for closed accounts in good standing reflect the credit bureaus' practice.

bloecke.md:
## Checking your own reports regularly

Looking at your own reports takes half an hour. It is the only way to find errors before they come to light, for example when you apply for an apartment. On AnnualCreditReport.com, the only official site for this, you can get your reports from all three bureaus free of charge, currently once a week. The most common findings are accounts that belong to someone with a similar name, wrongly reported late payments, paid debts still shown as unpaid and accounts listed twice. Rarer, but expensive, are accounts that someone else opened in your name.

schritte.text: Use AnnualCreditReport.com and request the reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, because creditors do not always report to all three. The report contains the complete data, not necessarily a score.
Look out for unknown accounts, wrong addresses, late payments you did not make, debts shown as unpaid and duplicate entries. Note down every irregularity with the date.

Dispute the entry with the credit bureau in writing or online, with copies of your evidence, and at the same time with the creditor that reported it. The bureau generally has to investigate within 30 days and delete or correct information it cannot verify.

If a dispute is not resolved, you can submit a complaint to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). For accounts that a stranger opened in your name, file a report at IdentityTheft.gov and place a fraud alert, so that creditors and the bureaus have to treat the accounts as fraud.

A credit freeze at all three bureaus is free and prevents new accounts from being opened in your name. You lift it temporarily, for example for a few days, when you apply for a loan or an apartment yourself.

bloecke.md:
## Applying for an apartment

Landlords and property managers usually run tenant screening: a credit report, eviction records and often a background check. You usually pay an application fee; some states and cities cap it or allow reusable screening reports. If a landlord rejects you or asks for a higher deposit because of a report, they must give you an adverse action notice naming the company that provided it, so you can check it for errors. The federal Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability; many states and cities protect additional characteristics, for example the source of your income.

bloecke.md:
## Preparing for emergencies

Creditworthiness is the part of keeping your finances in order that others can see. The other part is the question of whether your finances still work when you cannot act yourself, for example in hospital, after an accident, after a death or when strangers have taken over one of your logins. Such situations arise suddenly. Medical bills are an example: according to the CFPB, medical debt has been the most common type of debt in collections on credit reports, even though much of it stems from billing and insurance problems rather than unwillingness to pay.

bloecke.titel: Power of attorney and beneficiaries for bank accounts
bloecke.md:
Being married does not give you the right to manage your spouse's individual accounts. If someone becomes incapacitated without a **durable financial power of attorney**, relatives may have to ask a court to appoint a guardian or conservator, which takes time and costs money while bills continue. Many banks prefer or require their own form, so check whether your bank accepts the power of attorney.

A power of attorney ends at death. After that, only the executor can act, and only after the probate court has issued letters testamentary, which can take weeks to months. A **payable-on-death (POD)** designation on bank accounts and a **transfer-on-death (TOD)** designation on brokerage accounts close this gap: the money goes directly to the named beneficiaries outside probate. A joint account with right of survivorship also passes automatically, but it gives the co-owner full access during your lifetime and can expose the money to the co-owner's creditors. The inheritance side is covered in the lesson on partnership, children and inheritance.

- Overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases may only be charged if you have opted in. Without opting in, such transactions are simply declined. A buffer of one monthly payment in your checking account is cheaper than any fee.
- You can stop recurring electronic debits from your account by telling your bank at least three business days before the scheduled date; also revoke the authorization with the company.
- Report a lost debit card or unauthorized transfers at once. Within two business days, your liability is limited to $50, within 60 days of the statement to $500; after that, losses can be unlimited (Regulation E). For credit cards, liability is capped at $50 by law, and the card networks often waive even that.
- Go through recurring charges and subscriptions once a year, ideally together with checking your credit reports.

bloecke.titel: Protecting your brokerage account against fraud
bloecke.md:
A brokerage account cannot be stolen like a card, but it can be emptied just like a bank account. Four rules help against this.

- Use a separate email address for your bank and broker that you use nowhere else. Use each password only once and manage them in a password manager.
- Prefer an authenticator app or a security key to codes by text message. A SIM swap, in which criminals take over your phone number, is all it takes to intercept text codes. Ask your mobile carrier for a port-out PIN or number lock.
- Never share a code or approve a login at the request of others. Neither the bank nor the broker nor the police will ask for a one-time code or remote access to your computer. Name a trusted contact person with your broker, whom the firm may contact if it suspects fraud or diminished capacity.
- Keep trade confirmations and year-end tax forms. Brokers track the cost basis only for shares bought in recent years; for older holdings, missing purchase records can lead to an expensive tax problem when you sell or transfer.

bloecke.titel: Second-chance accounts and protection from garnishment
bloecke.md:
A negative record with ChexSystems can make it hard to open a checking account. Many banks and credit unions offer **second-chance accounts**, and accounts certified under the Bank On standards have low costs and no overdraft fees. Once you can open a regular account again, you should switch.

If a creditor garnishes your account, certain federal benefits are protected. When Social Security, Supplemental Security Income, VA benefits or federal retirement benefits are deposited directly, the bank must automatically protect two months' worth of these deposits (31 CFR Part 212). For wage garnishment by ordinary creditors, federal law limits the amount to the lesser of 25% of disposable earnings or the amount by which weekly earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage (15 U.S.C. § 1673). Higher limits apply to child support, taxes and federal student loans, and many states protect more.

mitnehmen: Credit bureaus store accounts and payment behaviour, but neither income nor savings, so your score depends on behaviour, not on prosperity.
For $15,000 over five years, several thousand dollars in interest separate excellent from fair credit; that is how much a weak score can cost.
Three measures cost nothing: using prequalification with soft inquiries, keeping your oldest card open and checking your free reports from all three bureaus regularly.
Negative entries generally disappear after seven years from the original delinquency, bankruptcies after up to ten; a credit freeze protects against accounts opened in your name.

Keeping your finances in order includes a durable power of attorney, payable-on-death or transfer-on-death designations, an emergency folder without passwords, separate logins and no codes shared at the request of others.

begriffe.text: Record kept by a credit bureau of a person's credit accounts, balances, payment history, collections, bankruptcies and inquiries. In the US, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion each keep one; reports are free at AnnualCreditReport.com.
The most widely used credit score in the US, usually on a scale from 300 to 850. It is calculated from the credit report, above all from payment history and amounts owed, and exists in many versions.

Entry made when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit. It can lower the score slightly and stays on the report for two years. Checking your own credit and prequalification create soft inquiries without effect.
Free block at a credit bureau that prevents new creditors from accessing your report, so that accounts cannot easily be opened in your name. You can lift it temporarily at any time.
Notice a lender or landlord must give if it denies an application or offers worse terms because of a consumer report. It names the reporting company and entitles you to a free copy of the report.

Beneficiary designation on a bank account (POD) or brokerage account (TOD) under which the assets pass directly to the named person on death, without probate. It does not give the beneficiary any access during your lifetime.
